analysis.one_liner: Charges the largest fossil fuel companies $1 trillion for past emissions to fund climate disaster recovery and resilience.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2024 with 22 cosponsors, all Democrats, and referred to three House committees. No committee acted on it and it never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would impose a one-time tax totaling $1 trillion on the fossil fuel companies most responsible for America's carbon emissions, based on peer-reviewed estimates of each company's share of carbon dioxide released from 2000 through 2022. Companies responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of emissions would pay a proportional share, with payments spread over up to nine years. The money would go into a dedicated federal fund for climate disaster recovery, resilient infrastructure, and adaptation, with 40% reserved for communities hit hardest by pollution and climate damage.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities facing climate-driven floods, hurricanes, heat waves, and wildfires — at least $15 billion a year for FEMA disaster response and resilience programs, $6 billion a year for community air-quality and climate grants, and 40% of all fund spending reserved for environmental justice communities, which the bill defines as communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities overburdened by fossil fuel pollution.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a $1 trillion Polluters Pay Climate Fund, financed by a one-time assessment on companies responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions between 2000 and 2022, payable by September 30, 2025 or in up to nine annual installments.

Directs the fund toward climate resilience and adaptation: at least $15 billion per year for FEMA disaster response and resilience programs, including at least $3 billion for the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities program, and at least $6 billion per year for Clean Air Act climate grants.

Reserves 40% of each year's fund spending for investments benefiting environmental justice communities, defined as communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities facing disproportionate pollution and climate harm.

Preserves the right of states, local governments, Tribes, and individuals to sue fossil fuel companies for climate damages and deception — the federal assessment cannot be used to offset court awards or as evidence in those cases, and it does not preempt state climate laws.

analysis.who_pays: The fossil fuel companies — coal, crude oil, and gas producers and refiners — each determined responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions during 2000–2022, including their successors. The tax is not deductible, and joint and several liability applies within controlled corporate groups.
analysis.who_pays_short: The largest fossil fuel producers and refiners

drawbacks.text: A one-time $1 trillion assessment on companies' past legal operations is unprecedented, and companies would pass some of the cost to consumers through fuel prices — the bill offers no mechanism to shield households from that.

The assessment applies retroactively to emissions from 2000 to 2022 based on the company's share of covered emissions, raising a fairness objection for companies that operated lawfully under the rules in effect at the time; the bill's own findings state the assessment is not a determination of fault.
Funds are spent subject to annual appropriations Acts, so a future Congress could decline to appropriate money even after the tax is collected.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directs a very large sum — $1 trillion — toward disaster recovery, resilient infrastructure, and communities most exposed to climate harm, paid by the companies whose products generated the emissions. The honest objections are that a retrospective $1 trillion levy is legally untested, that some costs would reach consumers through fuel prices, and that spending depends on future appropriations. No committee ever weighed those trade-offs publicly, because the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees — Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce — none of which took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on September 12, 2024, with 17 original cosponsors.
The Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce committees for consideration of provisions within each committee's jurisdiction.
No further action was recorded: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote. The bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest fossil fuel companies — coal, oil, and gas producers and refiners that would have owed the assessment — are better off, because no payment was ever collected and the obligation lapsed with the bill. Taxpayers and climate-vulnerable communities, who would have received the funded resilience and disaster programs, gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on September 12, 2024.

for.name: 22 House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Raskin, Schakowsky, Ocasio-Cortez, Grijalva, and Tlaib
for.what_they_did: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House committees (Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure)
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to all three committees on introduction day; none scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill died in committee.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Held the House majority and committee chairmanships in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: No member of the House majority sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and no committee under majority control advanced it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats and the sole sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican supported the bill, and with Republicans controlling House committees in the 118th Congress it never moved.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel producers and refiners (coal, crude oil, natural gas)
industries.note: Companies responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of CO2 from 2000–2022 would owe a share of a $1 trillion assessment, not deductible and with joint and several liability across corporate groups — a direct transfer from industry shareholders to public climate programs. Because the bill died, no payment was ever owed.

industries.industry: Government disaster response and resilience programs (FEMA, EPA grant programs, state and local infrastructure)
industries.note: The fund would channel at least $15 billion a year to FEMA and at least $6 billion a year to Clean Air Act climate grants, with 40% of spending reserved for environmental justice communities.

industries.industry: Households facing fuel and energy costs
industries.note: To the extent companies pass the assessment into fuel prices, consumers would bear some of the cost — a real objection supporters would have to answer.
